Lessons.Title: Modeling with Linear Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning aims: identify model inputs and outputs, translate verbal descriptions into affine equations, use diagrams for quantities and spatial measurements, and build/solve systems to compare practical choices.
The statement 'starts at b and gains m per unit' corresponds to y=mx+b. Explain the rate and initial value with units.
Two data points identify the linear slope. Check whether the resulting formula should apply only within a specific time interval or other realistic domain.
Geometric modeling may require a Pythagorean distance formula before simplification. Distances, times and cardinal directions must retain their units.
Competing plans should be compared as two functions of the same input variable. Their break-even point solves C1(x)=C2(x), but preferring one plan requires evaluating the appropriate inequality.

Independent Edulytics cool-down: (a) A supply model has $125 fixed cost and $3 per unit. Find C(40). (b) A population is 600 in year0 and 750 in year3; find P(t). (c) Compare A(d)=20+2d with B(d)=60+d and find when B saves money.
Independent Try It 1 — Model fixed and variable manufacturing cost. A workshop pays $30,000 rent and $0.40 for each item. Write cost C(n), initial value and units.
Independent Try It 2 — Forecast and threshold from a two-year trend. A town has 20,000 people in 2020 and 24,000 in 2024. Under a linear continuation find 2026 population and year of 30,000.
Independent Try It 3 — Use perpendicular projection geometry. Road segment points from town A=(0,0) to B=(30,40) km. Find travelled straight-line length to a junction at (12,16).

WorkedExamples.Title: Extrapolate population using a linear model
WorkedExamples.Question: A town has 7,500 people at t=0 and 8,700 at t=4 years. Assume a linear model. Find P(t) and forecast the year t=8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Steps: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Slope 300 residents/year; P(t)=7500+300t; P(8)=9900. Valid only if the linear trend persists.
Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Slope 300 residents/year; P(t)=7500+300t; P(8)=9900. Valid only if the linear trend persists.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Model perpendicular walking paths
WorkedExamples.Question: Two people start together; one walks east 6 km/h and another north 8 km/h. Build a function for the straight-line separation after t hours.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Steps: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Distance d(t)=√((6t)²+(8t)²)=10t km for t≥0, a linear distance model.
Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Distance d(t)=√((6t)²+(8t)²)=10t km for t≥0, a linear distance model.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Geometric projection in a road network
WorkedExamples.Question: A straight route to a location 40 km east and 30 km north has a total length 50 km. Find the projection of a point (16,12) on the route and its distance along the line.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Steps: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
The point lies at two-fifths of the route, so distance from start =20 km; slope 3/4 from coordinates.
Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The point lies at two-fifths of the route, so distance from start =20 km; slope 3/4 from coordinates.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose between two affine service plans
WorkedExamples.Question: Plan A charges fixed $40 and $1.50 per kilometre; plan B $75 and $0.80/km. Find the break-even travel distance and preferred plan afterward.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
Steps: Plan: Identify the independent input, create an equation or geometric relationship, and check units and constraints.
40+1.5d=75+0.8d; d=50 km; B cheaper for d>50.
Validate: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 40+1.5d=75+0.8d; d=50 km; B cheaper for d>50.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify known data points and contextual interpretation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Identify variables
KeyConcepts.Definition: The independent quantity is the controllable input and the dependent quantity changes with it.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose units and realistic nonnegative domain.
KeyConcepts.Example: Number of items n → cost C(n).

KeyConcepts.Title: Constant-rate model
KeyConcepts.Definition: Linear model y=mx+b when the rate Δy/Δx is constant.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Estimate m from two observed points, then determine b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Extrapolation caveat
KeyConcepts.Definition: Forecasting a linear trend beyond observations assumes the rate stays unchanged.
KeyConcepts.Rule: An extrapolation is a model forecast, not a guaranteed fact.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph and geometry model
KeyConcepts.Definition: Perpendicular displacement components can form a right triangle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Pythagorean length may simplify to a linear time function.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel/perpendicular route
KeyConcepts.Definition: Coordinate geometry can express route slopes and projection points.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use dot product or right-angle geometry for perpendicular lines.

KeyConcepts.Title: System of linear models
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two competing cost plans meet at equal cost.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Solve C1(x)=C2(x), then compare the two sides of threshold.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intercept and rate in context
KeyConcepts.Definition: A model's intercept is its value at input zero.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State both quantities in physical/financial units.
KeyConcepts.Example: Rent is $30,000 even if zero items produced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain/range and units
KeyConcepts.Definition: A realistic function may be limited to the duration of a measured trend.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not extrapolate a nonnegative population into negative numbers.
KeyConcepts.Example: Restrict t and explain model horizon.

Visuals.Title: First-party two-plan cost comparison
Visuals.Description: The lower-cost plan changes after equality at 50 km.

SummaryPoints: Use constant slope and intercept to build a model.
Confirm the chosen physical domain and extrapolation assumptions.
A geographic diagram can reveal lengths and perpendicular relationships.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Linear models can break beyond observed conditions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State model assumptions and plausible horizon.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing two prices with different input units.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Both expressions must use the same independent quantity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert to one shared variable and unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a positive break-even equality as the cheaper-plan interval.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equality alone says neither plan is cheaper.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Solve a strict inequality for preferred option.
